---
title: Memcached cache
description: MemcachedCache wraps `memjs` for distributed caching via Memcached. Smaller memory footprint than Redis, simpler protocol, no persistence (rebuilds on restart). Right when you already run Memcached.
---

`MemcachedCache` is the **Memcached-backed** Cache
implementation.  Distributed cache across pods, shared across
processes.

```ts
import { MemcachedCache, MemcachedCacheOptions } from 'actor-ts/cache';

const memcachedCacheOptions = MemcachedCacheOptions.create().withServers('memcached-1:11211,memcached-2:11211');
const cache = new MemcachedCache(
  memcachedCacheOptions,
);
```

## When to use Memcached

Two main reasons:

1. **Existing Memcached infrastructure** — your team runs it
   already.
2. **Pure cache use case** — you don't need Redis's extra
   features (persistence, pub/sub, scripting, sorted sets).

Memcached is **simpler than Redis** — fewer features, smaller
operational footprint, smaller memory overhead.  For pure
key-value caching with TTLs, it's plenty.

## Configuration

```ts
type MemcachedCacheOptionsType = {
  servers?:   string;                // comma-separated, default 'localhost:11211'
  username?:  string;
  password?:  string;
  keyPrefix?: string;                // server-side, applied to every operation
  client?:    MemcachedClientLike;   // pre-built memjs client
};
```

`memjs` (the underlying client) supports SASL auth via
`username`/`password`.  Multiple servers are hash-distributed.

## From config alone

The framework registers the Memcached factory itself, so a cache comes up
on Memcached with no `registerCache` call and no `new MemcachedCache(...)`
anywhere in your code — just a plugin id and a block:

```hocon
actor-ts.cache {
  sessions.plugin = "actor-ts.cache.memcached"   # cache('sessions') is Memcached

  memcached {
    servers    = "memcache-a:11211,memcache-b:11211"
    username   = ${?MEMCACHED_USERNAME}
    password   = ${?MEMCACHED_PASSWORD}
    key-prefix = "my-app:"
  }
}
```

The leaves are the kebab-case of the `MemcachedCacheOptionsType` fields
above.  `servers` is **one comma-separated string**, not a list, because
that is what `memjs`'s `Client.create` takes.

**An empty string means unset.**  `username`, `password` and `key-prefix`
ship as `""` so you can see the shape of the key; the reader drops them
rather than handing them on, and an empty `servers` falls through to the
built-in `localhost:11211` instead of being refused.

Each named cache can have its own connection settings, layered over the
global block leaf by leaf:

```hocon
actor-ts.cache {
  memcached.servers = "memcache-a:11211"

  sessions { plugin = "actor-ts.cache.memcached", memcached.key-prefix = "sess:" }
}
```

`memjs` is a lazy optional peer, so the block costs nothing until a cache
actually resolves onto it: the driver is imported on the first cache
*operation*, not at startup.

## Peer dependency

```bash
npm install memjs
# or: bun add memjs
```

## What works

| Cache method | Memcached implementation |
| --- | --- |
| `get`/`set`/`delete` | Direct Memcached commands. |
| `incr` | Memcached `INCR`/`ADD` combination. |
| `setIfAbsent` | Memcached `ADD` (atomic). |
| `mget`/`mset` | Parallel single-key operations. |

`mget`/`mset` aren't single-round-trip on Memcached (no
multi-key commands).  The framework parallelizes the
individual operations.

## Memcached vs Redis

| Aspect | Memcached | Redis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory overhead per entry | Lower | Higher |
| Multi-key operations | Slower (parallel single-key) | Faster (MGET, MSET) |
| Persistence | None | RDB / AOF available |
| Pub/sub | No | Yes |
| Data types | String only | Strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets |
| Cluster support | Client-side hashing | Built-in clustering |
| Replication | No (or via sidecars) | Built-in replication |

For pure cache: **either works**.  Redis wins for **almost
everything else** the framework might want.  Memcached wins for
**minimum operational footprint** when caching is the only need.

## Eviction

```ts
// Memcached configured with --memory-limit=2048 (MB)
// → LRU eviction once full
```

Memcached's eviction is **LRU**, configured at the
Memcached-server level (not from the cache client).  No
client-side eviction policy.

For a fixed-size cache, this is fine — Memcached drops old
entries to make room.

For anything carrying a **guarantee** it is not.  `InMemoryCache`
evicts entries that carry none before it touches a lock, a
rate-limit counter or an idempotency record; there is no
equivalent here, because the decision is made in the server and
the client is not consulted.  So an entry written by `setIfAbsent`
can disappear with most of its TTL left — a lock handed out twice,
a limit reset, a retry that re-runs its handler — and nothing in
the API reports it.  Size the Memcached instance for the guarantees
it holds, keep it off the same instance as a key space callers can
enumerate, and see
[what eviction protects and what it does not](/cache/in-memory/#what-eviction-protects-and-what-it-does-not)
for what the guarantee rests on.  This is separate from the
topology hazard below: that one needs a server to join or leave,
this one needs only memory pressure.

## Connection pooling

`memjs` maintains its own connection pool; the framework
doesn't manage it directly.  Tune via memjs options if needed
(usually defaults are fine).

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<Aside type="caution" title="No persistence">
  ```bash
  # systemctl restart memcached
  # → entire cache gone
  ```
  Memcached has zero persistence.  Treat caches as
  rebuild-from-source — never store anything you can't
  recompute.
</Aside>

<Aside type="caution" title="No multi-key atomic operations">
  ```ts
  // Two operations: read A, set B based on A → race possible
  ```
  Memcached doesn't have transactions / atomic multi-key
  operations.  For "atomic counter + check" patterns, the
  framework's `incr` and `setIfAbsent` are the only atomic
  primitives.
</Aside>

<Aside type="caution" title="Memcached cluster scaling">
  ```ts
  servers: 'm1:11211,m2:11211';
  // Adding m3: keys rebalance via consistent-hashing — some cache misses during the rebalance
  ```
  Memcached scaling requires client-side consistent-hashing
  awareness.  `memjs` handles it; expect a brief cache-miss
  spike when the cluster topology changes.
</Aside>

<Aside type="caution" title="ADD is atomic per server, not per cluster">
  ```ts
  servers: 'm1:11211,m2:11211';
  // 'lock:job' hashes to m1 — ADD there is atomic, so one caller wins
  // Add m3: the key may rehash to a server that has never seen it
  // → setIfAbsent('lock:job') succeeds a second time, while the first
  //   holder still believes it holds the lock
  ```
  Memcached has no cluster-wide coordination.  `ADD` is atomic on
  **the one server a key hashes to**, which is what makes
  `setIfAbsent` and `acquireLock` correct in steady state — every
  contender for a given key reaches the same server.  A **topology
  change breaks that assumption**: `memjs` rehashes the keyspace,
  the key can land on a different server with no entry for it, and
  the lock is handed out twice.

  There is no client-side fix — the framework cannot detect a
  rehash without reaching into memjs's internal hashring, which is
  precisely the detail memjs exists to hide.  If you use
  `acquireLock` on Memcached, either keep the server list fixed for
  the lifetime of the lock, or treat a double-grant as possible and
  guard the resource with a fencing token.  **Redis is the better
  backend for locking**; Memcached locks are best kept to
  optimisations where a duplicate run costs time, not correctness.
</Aside>
